newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Aborigines see sorcery, genocide in suicide law.
newsitem.headline: Aborigines see sorcery, genocide in suicide law.

text.p: Australia's world-first euthanasia law aroused the spectre of genocide and sorcery among Aborigines and could scare indigenous Australians away from life-saving health care, a special inquiry warned on Thursday.
Parliament's upper house Senate ordered one of its committee report on the voluntary euthanasia issue before a vote this month on a bill quashing the suicide law in the outback Northern Territory.
Four people have committed medically-assisted suicide since the Territory's law came into operation last July, the last of them a 70-year-old Sydney woman who died at the weekend.
The report said there were concerns about the law's impact on the territory's large Aboriginal population, which committee chief Eric Abetz said overwhelmingly opposed euthanasia.
Abetz's committee made no recommendations because politicians are allowed a conscience vote on this issue rather than being bound by party lines.
But it said Aboriginal communities opposed the controversial right to die law and may be driven away from quality health services through fear of dying.

"Aboriginal attitudes to euthanasia may have been affected by a belief that the western health system was part and parcel of a generally antagonistic culture which, with the additional spectre of euthanasia, could lead to the further demise or even genocide of Australian Aborigines," the report said.
"During the course of the inquiry, a major concern emereged whether the Northern Territory legislation may impact on the willingness of aborigines to access medical services."
One Aboriginal elder, leading anti-euthanasia campaigner Djiniyini Gondarra, told the inquiry many Aborigines already feared white doctors as sorcerers.
"When one of our people die, especially in hospital or after a big operation, the majority of our people believe that western doctors are Galka (sorcerers)," Gondarra said.
He told the committee he knew of people refusing to go to hospital because of fear of euthanasia.
Isolated Aboriginal communities in the Northern Territory live a largely traditional lifestyle, with little contact with the rest of the community.
Conservative government backbencher Kevin Andrews, backed by Prime Minister John Howard, has moved a bill for parliament to over-ride the territory law and end voluntary euthanasia.
The Andrews bill has already passed the lower house, the House of Representatives, with overwhelming support.
But its fate in the Senate is less clear.
The Senate is due to debate the issue and vote on the Andrews bill later this month.

The measure has been widely criticised by political, religious, Aboriginal and medical leaders, although opinion polls show 75 percent of Australians support the right to die for terminally-ill people.
But 93 percent of the almost 13,000 submissions to the inquiry opposed assisted suicides.
Although technically illegal throughout the rest of Australia, doctors say euthanasia is widely practised.
The territory law allows terminally-ill patients who meet strict conditions, including approval by three doctors, to commit suicide by lethal injection or pills.
